Privacy Policy

Effective November 18, 2026

Sajad ("the maintainer") maintains Tuxport, an Android app for running a Linux command-line environment on your device. This policy explains how Tuxport handles information, uses Android permissions, and lets you control your data.

1. Overview

You do not need an online Tuxport account. Linux user accounts you create inside Tuxport belong to the local Linux environment.

Tuxport stores your Linux files, settings, saved terminal state, and diagnostic logs on your device. It does not automatically upload this content to me. Tuxport has no advertising or analytics SDKs, and I do not sell your personal data or use it for advertising.

Some features involve other services: Tuxport contacts software mirrors during setup, programs you run can use the network, and you can choose to share files or diagnostics. The sections below explain these cases.

2. Information processed on your device

  • Linux environment and files. Tuxport stores the installed distribution, packages, local user accounts, configuration, and files you create or import. Programs you run may store command history, credentials, or other information in that environment.
  • Terminal content and session state. Tuxport processes your input and program output to provide the terminal. It saves terminal snapshots, recent output, tab layout, local login names, and working directories so it can restore the terminal display after the app stops unexpectedly. Terminal content may contain sensitive information that you type or that a program displays.
  • Preferences. Tuxport stores settings such as appearance, screen-off running behavior, file access, privacy mode, and permission-prompt history to remember your choices.
  • Clipboard. Tuxport accesses clipboard text for paste operations and when a foreground terminal program requests to read it. For a program's read request, Tuxport reads the text to show a confirmation and passes it to the program only if you allow it. Copy operations and terminal programs can also place text on the system clipboard while Tuxport permits clipboard access.
  • Network configuration. Tuxport reads network status and routing information to support networking for the Linux environment.

3. Diagnostics and support

Tuxport keeps local logs to help diagnose setup failures, crashes, and runtime problems. These may include the Tuxport version, Android version, device manufacturer and model, CPU architecture, Linux distribution, timestamps, process names, paths, and error messages. An exported diagnostic archive can also include Android process exit records and an available crash or unresponsive-app trace.

The diagnostic exporter does not deliberately gather terminal transcripts, shell history, an environment-variable dump, or your Linux files. Error messages and system traces can still contain sensitive details. Review an archive before sharing it.

Tuxport does not send diagnostics automatically. When you use Export diagnostic logs, you choose whether to save an archive or share it with another app. That destination receives the archive you select and handles it under its own privacy practices.

If you contact me through the project's GitHub issues, I receive your message and any attachments you attach. I use them to respond to your request, investigate the issue, and maintain Tuxport. GitHub processes those messages to host the discussion. Please do not send passwords, private keys, or unrelated personal information.

4. Network connections and third parties

After importing a Linux system, Tuxport automatically requests small amounts of repository data from its configured mirrors to choose a responsive package source. For Alpine Linux these include Alpine's download service, Tsinghua University TUNA, the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), and Aliyun. For Debian these include Debian's download service, TUNA, USTC, and Aliyun. Choosing to install Debian also downloads its system image from GitHub's raw-content service.

These services receive your network IP address, the requested resource, and normal connection and HTTP request metadata. They may keep server logs under their own policies. Tuxport uses these connections to test download speed and retrieve software; it does not attach your terminal contents, Linux files, or diagnostic archive to those setup requests.

Programs you install or run can connect to servers, download packages, authenticate to services, or transmit files and other information. The data they send depends on those programs, your commands, and their configuration. This can continue in the background while the programs run. Use software and destinations you trust.

Opening a web link sends the address to your browser. Importing a file through Android's file picker gives Tuxport access to the selected file and its name; a cloud file provider may download it from its service. Sharing or saving a file gives the selected recipient or provider the content needed for that action.

Apart from the transfers described in this policy, Tuxport does not upload your local content to the developer. Third-party services control their own storage, retention, and processing locations, which may be outside your country.

5. Android permissions and access

  • Internet and network state (INTERNET, ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE): support Linux programs' network connections, system-image downloads, mirror speed checks, and network configuration. Android grants these without a runtime dialog. Without connectivity, network-dependent operations will not work.
  • Foreground service (FOREGROUND_SERVICE, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE): keep user-started terminal sessions and Linux programs running while you use another app. You can stop sessions using Tuxport's exit controls.
  • Notifications (POST_NOTIFICATIONS): show running session status, command completion, and errors. On Android 13 and later, Tuxport requests notification access through Android when you choose to enable it. You can decline or turn notifications off in Android settings and continue using the terminal, although you may miss alerts.
  • Wake lock (WAKE_LOCK): keep the CPU awake when needed by your screen-off running setting. Change Screen-off running in Tuxport settings to control this behavior.
  • Battery optimization exemption (REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS): let you ask Android to reduce battery restrictions that can interrupt long-running programs. You can decline the request or change Tuxport's battery settings later. Android may suspend or stop background work when restrictions apply.
  • Biometric authentication (USE_BIOMETRIC, and the compatibility permission USE_FINGERPRINT): use Android's authentication prompt for optional Privacy mode and protected actions such as exporting diagnostics in that mode. Android verifies your biometrics or screen-lock credential. Tuxport receives the authentication result, not your fingerprint, face template, PIN, pattern, or password.

Tuxport uses Android's file picker for imports and exports rather than requesting broad access to shared storage. It does not request Android permissions for your contacts, location, camera, microphone, SMS, or call logs.

Allow other apps to access files is a Tuxport setting, off by default. Enabling it exposes the Linux environment through Android's system file picker. Other apps can access files or folders you grant them; access outside the Linux home directory is read-only. Turning it off revokes grants and blocks further file access through this provider, but cannot retrieve copies already made or close file handles another app already holds.

6. Security

Tuxport keeps its internal files in Android's app-private storage and configures Android backup and device transfer to exclude its app data. File sharing uses Android's access grants. Privacy mode adds a system-authenticated app lock, restricts screen capture, hides notification details, and disables file-provider access. It does not stop running Linux programs or encrypt the Linux filesystem with a separate Tuxport password.

Tuxport uses HTTPS for its built-in mirror probes and system-image download, and verifies the downloaded system image against an expected checksum. Network traffic from programs you run depends on their protocols and configuration. In particular, the default Debian package repository configuration uses HTTP; Tuxport does not guarantee encryption for all guest traffic. Use encrypted protocols such as HTTPS or SSH when sending sensitive information.

7. Retention and deletion

  • Linux files and settings: remain on your device until you delete them, reset or replace the Linux system where applicable, clear Tuxport's app storage, or uninstall Tuxport. Resetting the Linux system removes that system's data, but is not a substitute for clearing all Android app storage.
  • Saved terminal state: updates as sessions run. Tuxport removes saved restoration state on a normal service exit, except when a later startup has not yet restored data from an earlier interrupted run. After an unexpected stop or incomplete restoration, saved state can remain until a later run replaces or clears it, or you clear app storage.
  • Local diagnostics: use size-limited rotating logs for the current and previous app process runs. New runs and log rotation replace older records; there is no fixed number of retention days. Cached export archives remain until Tuxport prunes them, Android clears the cache, or you clear app storage.
  • Support correspondence: I retain messages and attachments for as long as needed to resolve your request and related follow-up, then delete them unless a legal obligation requires further retention. You can request earlier deletion by opening an issue at the address below.

To remove Tuxport's local data, open Android Settings → Apps → Tuxport → Storage and choose Clear storage or Clear data, or uninstall Tuxport and choose to remove its data if Android offers that choice. Labels vary by device. These actions remove your local Linux environment and files, so save anything you want to keep first.

Copies you export, clipboard entries, emails, and information held by third-party apps or servers are outside Tuxport's local storage. Delete those copies at their destination or contact the recipient. I cannot remotely access or delete the files on your device or data held by services you use from the terminal.

8. Your choices and requests

You can manage notifications and battery access in Android settings, change Tuxport's file access and Privacy mode settings, choose which files to import or share, and stop programs that use the network. You do not have to send diagnostics or contact support to use Tuxport.

For personal information you have sent to me, you can request access, correction, or deletion by opening an issue in the project repository. I may ask for the minimum information needed to verify that the request concerns your correspondence. There is no online Tuxport account to close; deleting local Linux accounts and files is under your control.

9. Changes to this policy

I will publish changes on this page and update the date above. If a change requires additional notice or consent, I will provide it before applying the new data practice.

10. Contact

For privacy questions or requests about information you have sent to me, open an issue in the project repository:
